a: Titus Caesar
t: Titus, son of the new emperor
p: Titus is Vespasian's son, sent to end the war in Judea that his father began.
b: Tacitus calls him Caesar Titus, using Caesar as a title of the emperor's heir. His father Vespasian had been fighting the Jewish revolt and was now emperor. Josephus says Titus was helping his father set up the new government in Alexandria when the quarrel inside Jerusalem split into three groups (Jewish War 5.1.1), and that he then marched out of Caesarea with part of his forces (5.1.6). Suetonius says Vespasian left the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. The rest of Titus's career is told in the other books of the Histories; see the notes on 5:10 for how Tacitus says he came to be in Judea.

a: finish conquering Judea
t: Judea: the land of Jesus and of the apostles
p: Compared with the Bible: Judea is the Roman province where Jesus was born and taught. Tacitus gives its war from the Roman side.
b: Judea is the Roman name for the land of the Jews. Matthew puts Jesus' birth there: "Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea while Herod was king" (Matthew 2:1). Luke dates his ministry by the Roman governor: "Pontius Pilate was governing Judea" (Luke 3:1). Tacitus is telling how that province was finally crushed. Answers: Jesus had warned of this war. "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20), and "your enemies will put up a palisade of stakes against you" (Luke 19:43). Tacitus's siege story is lost at the break in the manuscript, but Josephus tells it in full (Jewish War 5-6). Some readers hold that Jesus' words in Luke 21 look at AD 70; others see them as also pointing beyond it (see the card on this chapter).
r: Matthew 2:1; Luke 3:1; Luke 19:41-44; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 24:1-2; Mark 13:1-2

a: the 5th, the 10th and the 15th
p: Three legions had fought under Vespasian; Titus added a fourth and detachments.
b: A legion was the Roman army's main unit, with several thousand soldiers. Josephus names the same core: three legions that had been with Vespasian, plus the 12th, the legion that had been beaten earlier under Cestius, whose men marched "with greater alacrity" to avenge it (Jewish War 5.1.6). He says the 5th came by Emmaus and the 10th by Jericho. Later the 10th camped on the Mount of Olives (5.3.5), the hill where Jesus gave his talk on the temple's fall (Matthew 24:3). Tacitus does not mention the Mount of Olives.

a: whom he'd brought from Alexandria
p: Tacitus and Josephus both say Titus drew men from Egypt.
b: Josephus says Titus brought 2,000 men picked from the armies at Alexandria, and 3,000 more from the guards on the Euphrates (Jewish War 5.1.6). Tacitus names the legions the Alexandria men came from. The 22nd/18th question is in the variant on this verse. The Alexandria detail also ties Titus to Egypt, where Tacitus will place the Jews' own beginnings (5:3). Josephus adds that Tiberius Alexander, once governor of Alexandria, served at Titus's side as an adviser (5.1.6); he is not named in this verse.

a: Agrippa and Sohemus
p: Compared with the Bible: this King Agrippa is the Agrippa before whom Paul spoke in Acts 25-26.
b: Tacitus names "Agrippa" as a king in Titus's army. Only one king Agrippa could be meant in the year 70: Agrippa II. His father, Agrippa I, died at Caesarea after he appeared before the crowd "On a set day" (Acts 12:21-23); Josephus says the occasion was a festival with shows in honor of Caesar (Antiquities 19.8.2). Josephus says Claudius gave the younger Agrippa the territory of Philip and other lands and that he had sisters named Drusilla and Bernice (Antiquities 20.7.1). Acts has "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), and Paul says to him, "you know well every custom and every debate among the Jews" (Acts 26:3). Same person? Very likely. Josephus ties the name, the title and the sisters together, and no other Agrippa was a king in 70. Agrees: Agrippa is a Roman ally even while ruling Jews. Sohemus has no Bible link.

a: a strong force of Arabs
p: Neighbors who hated the Jews supplied troops; the Bible knows Arab rulers of the same region.
b: Tacitus says the Arab troops brought the hatred that neighbors usually have. Josephus too puts "Arabians" and Syrians in Titus's camp (Jewish War 5.13.4). In the Bible's world the Arabs to the east and south were the Nabateans, whose king Aretas appears in Paul's escape from Damascus: "the governor under King Aretas had guards watching the city of the Damascenes" (2 Corinthians 11:32). That link is only background: Tacitus names no king here, and Paul's king Aretas lived years before this war.

a: not far from Jerusalem
t: Jerusalem, as the Romans first meet it
p: Compared with the Bible: the city Tacitus is about to describe is the Bible's Jerusalem.
b: Tacitus is about to describe Jerusalem and the war that ended in its fall. Other writers tell of Roman armies at the same walls: Cassius Dio on Pompey's assault, in which the temple was taken "only with difficulty" (Roman History 37.16), and Josephus on Titus (Jewish War 5-6). The Bible's Jerusalem begins as "Salem" (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2), becomes David's city, holds Solomon's temple and then the second temple, and is where Jesus was crucified. Jesus wept over it: "If only you too had recognized on this day what leads to peace!" (Luke 19:42). Tacitus calls it the nation's capital (5:8); the Bible calls the temple the place where God had put his name. See the topics on Jerusalem and the temple.

a: the last day of a famous city
p: Tacitus promised the end of Jerusalem, but the surviving text breaks off before it.
b: Tacitus says he is about to tell "the last day of a famous city" (Latin supremum diem) and so will first lay out its beginnings. The surviving Histories stop in the middle of a sentence at 5:26, in the Batavian revolt. So Tacitus's own account of the fall of Jerusalem is gone. Josephus's Jewish War, written by a Jew who served as a commander and then was held by the Romans, is the full surviving account (Books 5 and 6), and Suetonius adds a few lines (Titus and Vespasian). The Wikipedia summary dates the Histories to about 100-110 and says Book 5 covers the end of 69 and the start of 70.

a: refugees from the island of Crete
t: Story one: Cretan refugees and the name Jew
p: A Greek-style story derives the name Jew from Mount Ida in Crete. The Bible gives a different origin.
b: This is the first of five origin stories. It runs on a word game: the Idaei (people of Mount Ida) became the Iudaei (Jews). The Bible knows where the name comes from: Leah named her fourth son Judah, "That is why she named him Judah" (Genesis 29:35), and the people of the southern kingdom and later all the Jews took the name from him. Link strength: none; the sound match is chance. Crete does appear in the Bible, but as a different place with a different people (see the topic on Crete). Van der Horst's review of Bloch's study says that the origin stories are tied into the later chapters on customs: "the 6 different origo-versions each play a role in the later chapters on mores etc." (Antike Vorstellungen vom Judentum, as reviewed by van der Horst).

a: the Idaei, supposedly got the longer, foreign-sounding name Judaei
p: The Latin says the name was lengthened into a foreign one (aucto in barbarum cognomento).
b: The Latin is Idaeos aucto in barbarum cognomento Iudaeos vocitari. Barbarum here means "foreign", so the point is that outsiders stretched Idaei into Iudaei (Church and Brodribb have "a barbarous lengthening of the national name"). The Hebrew name is Yehudah, and its Greek form Ioudaios is what gives Latin Iudaeus.

a: led by Hierosolymus and Judas
p: Compared with the Bible: "Judas" is Judah; "Hierosolymus" is a made-up founder for Jerusalem.
b: "Hierosolymus" looks like a founder-hero made up for a city's name; built from the Greek form of Jerusalem (Hierosolyma). "Judas" is the Greek and Latin form of Judah, the same name as Jacob's fourth son (Genesis 29:35). Differs: in Genesis, Judah is a son of Jacob who lived in Canaan and went down to Egypt with his brothers when famine came (Genesis 42:1-2; Genesis 43:8; Genesis 46:28); Abram had done the same earlier (Genesis 12:10). He is not a leader of an Egyptian crowd sent out under a queen-goddess Isis. Link: the name Judah is real; the story around it is Egyptian-flavored legend. No source Tacitus names here is a Jewish one.
r: Genesis 29:35; Genesis 49:10; Genesis 12:10; Genesis 42:1-2; Genesis 43:8; Genesis 46:28

a: came from the Ethiopians
t: Story three: Ethiopians, and Moses' Cushite wife
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible's Cush is the land south of Egypt, and Moses married a Cushite woman. A possible faint echo.
b: The Greek "Ethiopia" renders the Bible's Cush (Genesis 10:6-8; Isaiah 18:1), the land south of Egypt. Tacitus puts the Jews' beginning there under a Greek-myth king, Cepheus. The Bible never places Israel's origin in Cush, but it does record that Moses "had married a Cushite woman" (Numbers 12:1). Josephus tells how Moses led Egypt's army against the Ethiopians and married Tharbis, the king's daughter (Antiquities 2.10.2). Spec (Claude's theory): Tacitus's "Ethiopian" origin may be a garble of Moses' link to Cush. Nothing in Tacitus says so; treat it as a guess. Differs: the Bible's main claim is that Israel came from Abraham, from Mesopotamia and Canaan, not from Cush.

a: Assyrian newcomers
t: Story four: Assyrians who took part of Egypt
p: Compared with the Bible: the closest of the five to Genesis, which starts Israel in Mesopotamia and takes it through Egypt.
b: This is the story nearest to the Bible's outline: a people from the east, short of land, who entered Egypt and then settled in "the Hebrew country" near Syria. Genesis has Abram's family leave Ur and settle at Haran (Genesis 11:31: "they went out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there"), Abram is called "Abram the Hebrew" (Genesis 14:13), and later Abraham's grandson's family goes down to Egypt in famine. Josephus, writing against Egyptian slanders, points to the Egyptian historian Manetho, who describes the "Shepherds" who ruled Egypt and then left for Jerusalem; Josephus accepts that these were his forefathers, who fed sheep and were called Captives because Joseph told Pharaoh he was a captive (Against Apion 1.14). In Manetho's words as Josephus quotes them, the Shepherds left Egypt and, "in fear of the Assyrians, who had then the dominion over Asia," built Jerusalem. That is a separate Assyrian link to Tacitus's fourth story. Differs: the Bible does not call Abraham's people "Assyrians", and says they were given Canaan by God, not that they "took part of Egypt." Verdict on the fit: a distant, distorted echo of the patriarchs, at best.

a: the Hebrew country
p: Latin Hebraeae terrae: the one place in the Histories where Tacitus uses the Hebrews' own word.
b: The Latin Hebraeasque terras uses the name "Hebrew", which the Bible gives Abram (Genesis 14:13) and which Pharaoh uses of Israel's women (Exodus 1:15-16 speaks of "the Hebrew midwives"). Searching the Latin of all five surviving books, Tacitus uses "Hebrew" only here, and not for the people he calls Judaei. The Latin has "Hebrew lands", not "Israel", so the translation does not put "Israel" in this verse.

a: the Solymi, a nation celebrated in Homer's poems
t: Story five: the Solymi of Homer
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible calls early Jerusalem "Salem"; Josephus says some link it to Homer's Solyma.
b: Homer's Solymi are a warrior people in Asia Minor (Livius.org's page on this passage gives Iliad 6.184 and 6.204 and Odyssey 5.283). The sound of "Solymi" fits "Hierosolyma", the Greek name of Jerusalem. The Bible's early name for the city is Salem: "Melchizedek king of Salem" (Genesis 14:18), and "His lair was in Salem, and his den in Zion" (Psalm 76:2). Josephus writes that in Abraham's time the city was called Solyma and adds that "some say that Homer mentions it by that name" (Antiquities 7.3.2). In Whiston's English, the words "Salem, or" before Solyma and a clause saying Homer named the temple Solyma are the translator's own additions, in square brackets, and are not counted here as Josephus's. Link strength: the name Salem is real; that Homer's Solymi are Jews is a guess by sound. It is the only one of the five stories where a Jewish writer and the Bible give any support to the name.

a: Most writers agree
p: Tacitus says most writers tell the plague-and-exile story. Josephus names the Egyptian writers who did.
b: Tacitus does not name them. Josephus does, in Against Apion: Manetho (a king named Amenophis expels lepers, who choose a priest Osarsiph, "or Moses", as ruler, 1.14-31), Cheremon, and Lysimachus (1.34). These are the writers Josephus wrote his book to answer. Van der Horst's review of Bloch says that for the rest Tacitus "does not offer really new information" but follows in general what his predecessors had written about the Jews, sometimes even including self-contradictory information, such as a worship with no image beside the worship of an ass. Tacitus's "most writers agree" is a Roman way of saying "this is the common story"; he does not vouch for it.

a: a disease broke out across Egypt
t: The plagues turned into a disease
p: Compared with the Bible: Exodus has ten plagues sent by the LORD; Tacitus has one disease and a king's cure.
b: In Exodus, plagues strike Egypt because Pharaoh will not let Israel go, and the Egyptians are hit, not Israel (see the topic on the plagues). Tacitus reverses it: the disease is among the exiles, and they are expelled. Josephus quotes Manetho and Lysimachus saying the Jews were "leprous and scabby" (Against Apion 1.34) and answers that if the story were true there could not be so many of them (1.35). Differs from Exodus at the root. Why a Roman could write it: Josephus names Egyptian writers (Manetho, Cheremon, Lysimachus) who told it; it is the opposite of the Jewish memory, told by rivals.

a: King Bocchoris
p: The name Bocchoris comes from Lysimachus's version, not from the Bible.
b: The Bible names no pharaoh at the Exodus, only "the king of Egypt" or "Pharaoh" (Exodus 1:15). Josephus quotes Lysimachus, who has the king Bocchoris send to the oracle of Hammon about a food shortage (Against Apion 1.34). Manetho's king is called Amenophis. Livius.org's page on this passage notes that the Bocchoris date is "too late." Tacitus has picked Lysimachus's king, with Lysimachus's oracle; but his version differs, since the oracle there tells the king to drown the leprous people.

a: the oracle of Hammon
p: Hammon is the Egyptian god Amun, whom the Greeks called Zeus-Ammon, in his oracle shrine.
b: Hammonis oraculum is the oracle of Ammon in the Libyan desert (the Greeks and Romans identified him with Zeus and Jupiter). Josephus quotes Lysimachus saying that Bocchoris sent to "[Jupiter] Hammon" (Against Apion 1.34). Tacitus has the oracle say to "purify his kingdom". In Exodus a very different voice tells Pharaoh: "Let my people go" is Moses' demand in the LORD's name (see Exodus 3:18 for the request to go three days into the wilderness).

a: one of the exiles, Moyses
p: Compared with the Bible: Tacitus's Moyses is the Bible's Moses, but made an exile who invents a religion.
b: Same person? Very likely: the name, Egypt, the wilderness, the water from a rock and the laws all line up, and Josephus treats the Egyptian Osarsiph and Moyses stories as slanders about Moses (Against Apion 1.26-31). Differs: in Exodus, Moses is a Hebrew raised in Pharaoh's house who flees to Midian (Exodus 2:15-22), then is sent back by the LORD (Exodus 3). He does not arise as an exile from a plague camp, and his laws come from God at Sinai (Exodus 20), not from his plan "to make sure of the nation's loyalty" (5:4). The grain of truth in "Moses the Egyptian": Pharaoh's daughter took the child and "he became a son to her" (Exodus 2:10), and Stephen says that "Moses was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22). Neither verse makes him a priest or an exile from a plague camp. Strabo, the Greek geographer, also calls Moses an Egyptian priest, but a good one who taught that God cannot be shown in any image (Geography 16.2.35). So the "Egyptian Moses" story could be friendly or hostile. See the topic on Moses.

a: take as their heaven-sent leader whoever first got them out of their present misery
t: A leader "from heaven" who is found, not sent
p: Claude's theory: Tacitus's "heaven-sent leader" turns the Bible's call of Moses upside down.
b: The Latin is sibimet duce caelesti crederent, primo cuius auxilio praesentis miserias pepulissent. Moses "warns" them that gods and men have deserted them, and tells them to follow whoever first rescues them. In Exodus, God first calls Moses at the burning bush and sends him (Exodus 3:10), and the people believe when they see the signs (Exodus 4:30-31). My reading (spec): Tacitus keeps the shape of a rescue under a divinely sent leader but removes God from the story: the "leader" is a man who comes forward in a crisis. That fits his habit, seen in 5:13, of explaining what he reports as human ambition or chance.

a: a herd of wild asses
t: Wild asses and the water from the rock
p: Compared with the Bible: Exodus has Moses strike a rock for water at God's word; Tacitus has him follow wild asses.
b: In Exodus 17, the people have no water, and God tells Moses to strike the rock at Horeb: "You will hit the rock, and water will flow out of it, and the people will drink" (Exodus 17:6). In Numbers 20, Moses strikes a rock again and "Water came out in plenty" (Numbers 20:11). Tacitus keeps the thirst, the rock and the plentiful water, but swaps the miracle for a clue: animals leading a clever man to a spring. Differs. The wild ass is not in either Bible story. Josephus records a charge that the Jews kept an ass's head of gold in the temple (Against Apion 2.7) and answers that Pompey and others who entered found nothing of the kind. Tacitus's ass, and his "effigy of the animal" in 5:4, join that slander to the thirst story.

a: opened up plenty of veins of water
p: Latin largas aquarum venas: plentiful veins.
b: The picture of springs as "veins" (venae) is the same picture Tacitus uses for the balsam tree in 5:6. Exodus 17:6 and Numbers 20:11 say the water came out of the rock; Numbers 20:11 stresses amount: "Water came out in plenty." That matches the Latin largas, "plentiful".

a: a nonstop journey of six days, and on the seventh
p: Compared with the Bible: the six-and-seven pattern makes a Sabbath story in the Greek and Egyptian versions Josephus answers.
b: Tacitus says they traveled six days and "on the seventh" took the land; in 5:4 he ties the Sabbath to this. In Exodus the Sabbath rests on creation: "in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth ... and on the seventh day he rested" (Exodus 20:11), and in Deuteronomy on the Exodus: "Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15). Josephus quotes the writer Apion, who said the Jews traveled six days, then had swellings in the groin and rested on the seventh, and Josephus mocks the explanation (Against Apion 2.2). Differs: Tacitus's journey has no Sinai, no forty years, and no Jordan crossing (Joshua 3).

a: drove out the people living there and took the land
p: Compared with the Bible: Tacitus compresses forty years and Joshua's wars into one sentence.
b: The Bible has Israel wander forty years and then cross the Jordan on dry ground: "all Israel crossed over on dry ground" (Joshua 3:17). The land is given as a promise to Abraham and carried out with war and with command to drive out the nations. Tacitus has no covenant, no promise, and no wilderness years. Agrees on the outcome: a people from Egypt ends up holding Judea. Differs on how and why. Josephus counts 612 years from the Exodus to Solomon's building of the temple (Against Apion 2.2), which Tacitus's "a city and a temple were dedicated" folds together.

a: where a city and a temple were dedicated
p: Compared with the Bible: Jerusalem's temple was built by Solomon centuries after Moses.
b: In the Bible, the tabernacle comes first, in the wilderness (Exodus 25-40). The temple at Jerusalem is built by Solomon (1 Kings 6), long after Moses, and Solomon says, "I have built you a princely house" (1 Kings 8:13). Tacitus runs the Exodus, the conquest and the temple together as one trip. Differs. See the topics on the temple and the tabernacle.

a: new rites, the opposite of what everyone else does
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible also says Israel's laws set it apart, but for holiness, not hatred.
b: Tacitus says Moyses made rites that reverse everyone else's, so that the people would stay loyal. The Bible agrees that the law sets Israel apart, and on purpose: "Keep yourselves holy, and be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44), and Israel is to be "a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). Esther 3:8 shows an enemy saying the same thing in a hostile way: "Their laws are unlike any other people's." Josephus reports that Manetho's Osarsiph also made laws "mainly opposite to the customs of the Egyptians" (Against Apion 1.26). Differs: the Bible says God gave the laws to a people already his (Exodus 19:5-6; Exodus 20), and sees the set-apart life as a calling, not a trick.

a: a statue of the animal that showed them the way
t: The golden calf and the ass
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible does record animal images in Israel's past, the golden calf and Jeroboam's calves, but as sins.
b: Tacitus says the Jews put the statue of the guiding animal (the wild ass) in the inner shrine. Josephus answers Apion's slander of an ass's head: Antiochus Epiphanes, Pompey, Crassus and Titus all took the temple and none "found any such thing there" (Against Apion 2.7). The Bible's best-known animal image in Israel's worship is Aaron's calf: "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (Exodus 32:4), which Moses judged a sin. King Jeroboam "made two calves of gold" for Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28-29), and Hezekiah crushed Moses' bronze snake because Israel burned incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). Differs: an animal image in the shrine is the opposite of the law: "You must not make yourself an idol" (Exodus 20:4). The law itself commanded two golden cherubim on the ark (Exodus 25:18-20), and Solomon's basin stood on twelve bronze oxen (1 Kings 7:25), so "no image" means no image of God, not no sculpture at all. Tacitus disagrees with himself: 5:4 puts an animal's statue in the shrine, while 5:5 says the Jews set up no statues and 5:9 says Pompey found an empty seat. Cassius Dio says the Jews "never had any statue of him even in Jerusalem itself" (Roman History 37.17).
r: Exodus 32:1-6; Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 4:15-19; 1 Kings 12:28-29; 2 Kings 18:4; Exodus 25:18-20; 1 Kings 7:25

a: They sacrifice a ram, as if to insult Hammon, and they sacrifice an ox too
p: Compared with the Bible: Israel did offer rams and oxen, but for the LORD, not to mock Egypt's gods.
b: The Bible's sacrifices include bulls, rams and lambs (Leviticus 1-7). The first Passover is a lamb or kid with the blood on the doorposts (Exodus 12), and on the night of the first Passover the LORD says, "on all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments" (Exodus 12:12). Tacitus says the ram insults Hammon and the ox insults Apis, the sacred bull of Egypt; that is his reading of the sacrifices, not something the Law says. The nearest Bible parallels show the Egyptians' own dislike, not an Israelite insult: Moses tells Pharaoh, "What we sacrifice to the LORD our God is a thing the Egyptians abhor" (Exodus 8:26), and Joseph tells his brothers to say they keep livestock because "Egyptians loathe every shepherd" (Genesis 46:34). Differs on the reason: the offerings are the LORD's own commands for atonement and thanks; their effect on Egypt's gods is a side result, not their aim. Josephus answers the writer Apion, who objected to sacrificing animals, that in doing so he "demonstrates himself to be an Egyptian" (Against Apion 2.14).

a: They avoid pork
t: No pork, and a skin disease
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible forbids pork as unclean, and gives no skin-disease reason.
b: "The pig has a split hoof, divided all the way through, but it does not chew the cud. It is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7), repeated in Deuteronomy 14:8. The reason the Bible gives is the rule about cloven hoof and cud, within a larger call to be holy. Tacitus gives an Egyptian-style reason: a disease the pig is prone to. Differs. Josephus meets the charge by saying Egyptian priests abstain from swine's flesh too (Against Apion 2.14). Pigs also mark a later fight over the Law: Antiochus's decree was "to sacrifice pigs and unclean animals" (1 Maccabees 1:47; see the note on Histories of Tacitus 5:8), and Isaiah condemns "those who eat the flesh of pigs" at forbidden rites (Isaiah 66:17; compare Isaiah 65:4). In the New Testament, Peter's vision tells him "What God has made clean, you must not call common" (Acts 10:15) and Mark adds that Jesus "made all foods clean" (Mark 7:19).
r: Leviticus 11:7-8; Deuteronomy 14:8; 1 Maccabees 1:47; Isaiah 66:17; Acts 10:13-15; Mark 7:18-19

a: frequent fasts
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible commands a yearly fast on the Day of Atonement; Tacitus says "frequent."
b: The Law names one yearly fast, the Day of Atonement: "you are to humble yourselves and do no work at all" (Leviticus 16:29). Later practice had more: Zechariah names four fasts, in the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months (Zechariah 8:19), and in a parable a Pharisee says, "Twice a week I fast" (Luke 18:12). Acts 27:9 speaks of "the Fast" as already past, which fits the autumn Day of Atonement (a reading, not stated in the verse). Tacitus explains the fasts as a memory of old hunger in the wilderness, whereas the Bible tells them as repentance and atonement. Josephus notes the high priest wears his plain clothes into the holy place on the one day a year "our custom is for all of us to keep a fast to God" (Jewish War 5.5.7).

a: Jewish bread, made with no yeast
t: Unleavened bread and the hurried grain
p: Compared with the Bible: Exodus does tell of dough carried out unrisen in a hurry; Tacitus has it close.
b: Tacitus says unleavened bread recalls grain "grabbed in a hurry." Exodus: "the people picked up their dough before it rose" and "baked the dough ... into round cakes of unleavened bread, because it had not risen. They had been driven out of Egypt and could not linger" (Exodus 12:34, 39). Deuteronomy calls it "the bread of hardship, because you came out of the land of Egypt in a rush" (Deuteronomy 16:3). Agrees on the haste and the meaning of the bread, which makes it the closest of Tacitus's explanations to the Bible. Differs: in Exodus it is an escape, not a theft of grain, and the festival is a command (Exodus 12:15). Josephus says John chose "the feast of unleavened bread" to seize the temple (Jewish War 5.3.1; see 5:12).

a: rest on the seventh day because it ended their labors
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible gives two reasons for the Sabbath, creation and the Exodus; Tacitus gives labor and, later, laziness.
b: Exodus: "in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them, and on the seventh day he rested" (Exodus 20:11). Deuteronomy: "Then your slave, man or woman, can rest just as you do" (Deuteronomy 5:14). Tacitus's "it ended their labors" is the nearest he comes, though he means Egyptian-era toil. The writer Apion said the word Sabbath came from a disease of the groin, and Josephus calls this a trifle (Against Apion 2.2). Differs: Tacitus calls Sabbath rest laziness; the Bible calls it a gift (Mark 2:27: "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings"). Christians differ on how the Sabbath binds today (see the card on this chapter).

a: they gave the seventh year to laziness too
p: Compared with the Bible: Leviticus 25 gives a rest year for the land, and the poor eat from it.
b: "In the seventh year the land is to have a Sabbath of complete rest" (Leviticus 25:4); Exodus 23:11 adds that the needy "can eat from it", and what is left, "the wild animals can eat." The seventh year has two aims: rest for the land and food for the poor. Tacitus sees only idleness. This is one of the clearest places where a Roman reader misses the law's reason. Differs. The topic on the Jubilee covers the practice in later history.

a: this honor is for Saturn
p: Some Romans linked Saturn's day, Saturday, with the Jews' rest. Tacitus lists two reasons without picking.
b: Tacitus gives two ways the Jews might have come to honor Saturn: the Idaei brought the cult (tying to 5:2), or Saturn's planet has the highest orbit and seven governs many heavenly cycles. The Bible has nothing like this; the Sabbath rests on God's rest (Exodus 20:11) and the seven-day week comes from creation week (Genesis 2:2-3 is the passage topic). Where the Bible mentions star worship, it forbids it: "do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). A star-god does appear in Israel's past, as a sin: "the star of your gods" in Amos 5:26 (with Sikkuth and Kiyyun) and "the star of the god Rephan" in Stephen's speech (Acts 7:43). The site makes no claim about which god or planet those names mean. Cassius Dio also calls the Jewish rest day "the day of Saturn" (Roman History 37.16-17). Link strength: none; this is Roman star-lore laid over the Jewish week.

a: multiples of seven
t: Seven stars that rule mortal lives
p: The seven "wandering stars" were the Sun, Moon and five planets, and Tacitus counts Saturn's the highest.
b: The Latin is septem sideribus, quis mortales reguntur: seven bodies that rule human affairs. For the ancients these were the Sun, the Moon and the five visible planets, and Saturn was the farthest out. The sentence shows the Roman idea that heavenly bodies steer human life. The Bible warns against worshiping them (Deuteronomy 4:19), mocks advisers "who stare at the stars" to announce what is coming (Isaiah 47:13), and tells Israel, "Do not panic at the signs in the sky" (Jeremiah 10:2). Cassius Dio, describing the custom of naming the days after the seven planets, says the Egyptians began it (Roman History 37.18).

a: they got their strength from that very wickedness
p: Tacitus says the other customs are "perverse and foul" and grew strong because of it. The Latin is blunt.
b: The Latin is cetera instituta, sinistra foeda, pravitate valuere. After conceding that the rites above are "defended by their age," he turns on the rest. This is Tacitus speaking in his own voice, not reporting a story. Van der Horst's review says Bloch shows that even features Tacitus does not present negatively, such as Jewish monotheism, "receive a non-positive colouring", and that one aim of the passage is to show "that the Jews fully deserved to be defeated and have their only temple destroyed by the Romans." How the site reads it: as a Roman outsider's view, set beside what the Law actually says. It is not a description of what Jews believed.

a: The worst people of other nations dropped their own religions and kept piling up tribute and gifts there
t: Money sent to the temple, and God-fearers
p: Compared with the Bible: the temple really drew money and worshipers from the nations and from Jews abroad.
b: Tacitus explains Jewish wealth this way. The New Testament shows what he saw from outside. Jews paid a yearly temple tax ("the men who collected the double drachma", Matthew 17:24). Gentiles who feared the God of Israel came to worship, such as the Ethiopian court official who "had come to Jerusalem to worship" (Acts 8:27), and the centurion Cornelius, who "feared God" (Acts 10:2), and Paul addresses "you who fear God" in a synagogue (Acts 13:16). Agrees that outsiders were drawn to the Jews' worship and gave to it. Differs in the verdict: Tacitus calls them "the worst people", the Bible calls them seekers.

a: their loyalty is stubborn and their pity is quick, but toward everyone else they feel hostile hatred
p: Compared with the Bible: the Law commands love of the foreigner. This charge of hostility to outsiders was common in the ancient world.
b: The Latin is apud ipsos fides obstinata, misericordia in promptu, sed adversus omnis alios hostile odium. The charge that Jews hated outsiders is old: Haman says to the king, "Their laws are unlike any other people's" (Esther 3:8). The Law commands the opposite, loving the foreigner (see the topic on foreigners), and Jesus sums up the second great command as love of neighbor (see the topic on love your neighbor). But there were Jews who held outsiders at a distance: Peter says it was "not allowed" for a Jew to keep company with a foreigner (Acts 10:28), and Paul rebukes Peter for drawing back from Gentile table fellowship (Galatians 2:12). So: the keeping apart is real, the hatred is Tacitus's reading of it. A Christian reader should weigh each claim separately, as the notes on this verse do.

a: They eat separately and sleep separately
p: Compared with the Bible: the food laws and meal rules did keep Jews from eating with outsiders.
b: Peter says "for a Jewish man, keeping company with a foreigner or visiting one is not allowed. But to me God has shown that no human being is to be called common or unclean" (Acts 10:28). Galatians 2:12 shows the same reluctance at Antioch. Agrees that Jews of the time kept apart at meals. Differs on why: the Law's purity rules and the call to be holy (Leviticus 11:44), not contempt. The New Testament breaks the barrier: "He made the two one, and he broke down the middle wall" (Ephesians 2:14).

a: keep away from foreign women
p: Compared with the Bible: the Law forbids marrying the Canaanite peoples; Ezra repeats it. Tacitus's "lust" charge has no Bible basis.
b: "Do not marry into their families" (Deuteronomy 7:3), because they would turn Israel's sons to other gods (Deuteronomy 7:4). Ezra's officials complain that Israel "failed to keep apart from the peoples of the lands" and "the holy seed has mingled" (Ezra 9:1-2). The Bible also has foreign women who join Israel, such as Ruth. Agrees that Jews avoided marrying outsiders. Differs: the reason is the faith, not the body, and the Bible forbids adultery and every sex act outside marriage strictly. Tacitus's words that "among themselves nothing is forbidden" are false to the Law (see the topic on marriage).

a: They set up circumcision so that they'd be recognized by the difference
p: Compared with the Bible: Genesis calls circumcision the sign of the covenant, which is a mark of difference. Tacitus gets the effect right.
b: God tells Abraham: "You are to cut away the flesh of your foreskin, and that will be the sign of the covenant between me and you" (Genesis 17:11), at eight days old (Genesis 17:12). Tacitus says the Jews made the custom "so that they'd be recognized," a purpose the Bible does not give; it gives God's command. Agrees that it marks them out. Differs on the origin: Abraham, about 2,000 years before Tacitus, not Moyses (5:4). Josephus notes that Egyptian priests were also circumcised (Against Apion 2.14), and Jeremiah lists Egypt with Judah, Edom, Ammon and Moab among the peoples "circumcised in a foreskin", adding that "all the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart" (Jeremiah 9:25-26). The New Testament debates it: some taught "If you are not circumcised as Moses' custom requires, you cannot be saved" (Acts 15:1); Paul says "circumcision is of the heart" (Romans 2:29). See the topic on circumcision.
r: Genesis 17:9-14; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Acts 15:1; Acts 16:3; Romans 2:25-29; Galatians 5:2

a: Those who cross over to their ways
t: Converts, proselytes and the scorn of the gods
p: Compared with the Bible: Jesus mentions the Pharisees' zeal to make one convert; converts did take up the Law.
b: Jesus says to the scribes and Pharisees: "You go around sea and dry land to make one convert" (Matthew 23:15). So converts were real, and Tacitus treats them as part of the Jewish danger. Tacitus says the first thing a convert learns is "to despise the gods, give up their country, and treat parents, children and brothers as worthless." Differs: the first command is "You must not have any other gods in my presence" (Exodus 20:3); the Law honors parents (Exodus 20:12). A convert did leave idols, which a Roman called despising the gods. Paul's sermon at Athens shows the same refusal in a Christian mouth: "we should not suppose that the Divine looks like gold or silver or stone" (Acts 17:29).

a: despise the gods, give up their country
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible denies the gods of the nations, and some Christians read them as real powers.
b: Bible: "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known" (Deuteronomy 32:17), and Paul: "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20). Christian readings (S lens): some read the nations' gods as nothing; others (the divine-council reading) as real fallen powers. See the topics on idolatry and the divine council. Tacitus's "despise" is how a Roman felt Jewish refusal to honor the gods of the state, which put Jews and later Christians in conflict with civic worship.

a: it's a crime to kill any of their newborn children
p: Compared with the Bible: the Law and Josephus say every child is to be raised; Tacitus is accurate.
b: Josephus: "The law, moreover, enjoins us to bring up all our offspring, and forbids women to cause abortion" (Against Apion 2.25). The Bible calls children a gift: "sons are an inheritance the LORD gives" (Psalm 127:3), and records the midwives who refused Pharaoh's order to kill the Hebrew boys (Exodus 1:15-17). Agrees. Tacitus and Josephus line up. Tacitus lists this as a Jewish custom set against others; the Law's care for every child matches the Bible's view of children as a gift.

a: the souls of those killed in battle or by execution are eternal
p: Compared with the Bible: Judaism of this age believed in life after death, but by different views.
b: Tacitus says Jews think the souls of those killed in battle or by execution are eternal, and that this explains their love of children and contempt for dying. Josephus makes a similar argument in his speech at Jotapata: "the soul is ever immortal, and is a portion of the divinity that inhabits our bodies" (Jewish War 3.8.5), and writes that the Essenes teach that souls are immortal (2.8.11). The Bible's hope is resurrection: "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up" (Daniel 12:2). The Sadducees denied it, and the Pharisees affirmed it (Acts 23:8). Partly agrees. Tacitus's claim fits the martyr stories: the faith that death in God's cause is not the end. See the topics on the soul and resurrection.

a: They bury their bodies rather than burning them
p: Compared with the Bible: burial is the biblical norm. Tacitus links it to Egypt.
b: Abraham buys a cave for Sarah (Genesis 23:19-20). Jacob and Joseph are embalmed in Egypt (Genesis 50:2-3; Genesis 50:26). The one burning in the books is Saul and his sons, whose bones were then buried (1 Samuel 31:12-13). Tacitus says Jews follow "the Egyptian custom" of burying and has the same care for the dead and the same belief about the underworld as Egypt, but opposite beliefs about the heavens. Agrees on burial; differs on the source: the Bible's burial customs come from the patriarchs. See the topic on burial.

a: the Jews understand only with the mind, and one divine power
t: One God, known by the mind
p: Compared with the Bible: this is the sentence in Tacitus closest to the Bible's creed. A fair witness to Jewish worship.
b: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Tacitus calls it one numen (divine power) grasped by the mind alone. The Greek geographer Strabo says Moses taught that God cannot be pictured by any image of beast or human (Geography 16.2.35). Agrees in substance. Even a hostile Roman states the Jewish creed correctly here. The next sentences in Tacitus carry the Bible's argument against idols, though Tacitus does not credit it. See the topic on monotheism.

a: make images of God in human form out of perishable materials
p: Compared with the Bible: the second commandment and Paul at Athens say the same.
b: "You must not make yourself an idol, or the form of anything up in the sky, or down on the earth, or in the waters below the land" (Exodus 20:4); "You saw no form of any kind on the day the LORD spoke to you at Horeb" (Deuteronomy 4:15). Paul at Athens: "we should not suppose that the Divine looks like gold or silver or stone, a carving shaped by human craft and invention" (Acts 17:29). Josephus: no material, however costly, is fit for an image of God (Against Apion 2.23). Agrees. Christians divide on images of Christ and the saints (see the card on this chapter).

a: So they put up no statues in their cities, let alone in their temples
p: Josephus says the Law forbids images; Tacitus's claim fits the temple Pompey entered.
b: Josephus says the Law forbids making images, and the Jews who protested the emperor Gaius's order to set his statue in the temple were ready to die (Against Apion 2.6; see the note on 5:9 about Gaius, whom Tacitus's Latin calls Caesar and the translation calls Caligula). Josephus says that in the inmost room of the temple of his day "there was nothing at all" (Jewish War 5.5.5). Tacitus's statement here sits badly with his earlier claim of an animal effigy in the inner shrine (5:4).

a: They don't pay this flattery to their kings, or this honor to the emperors
p: Compared with the Bible: Jews and Christians refused to treat the emperor as a god, but paid taxes.
b: The Latin is non regibus haec adulatio, non Caesaribus honor: no statues for kings, no such honor to the Caesars. Jews sacrificed for the emperor but would not worship him, and the Gaius crisis is the sharpest case (see 5:9). The Gospels give Jesus' line when asked about the tax: "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Mark 12:17). Christians in Thessalonica were charged with breaking "Caesar's decrees by saying that Jesus is another king" (Acts 17:7), and the chief priests said before Pilate, "We have no king except Caesar" (John 19:15). See the topics on the imperial cult and church and state. Agrees that the refusal was real.

a: their priests sang to flutes and drums, were wreathed in ivy, and a golden vine was found in the temple
t: Priests, ivy and the golden vine
p: Compared with the Bible: the temple had a golden vine in Josephus's account, and the Bible's own vine is Israel.
b: Tacitus says some people took the flutes, drums, ivy and golden vine as signs that the Jews worshiped Father Liber (the Roman Dionysus or Bacchus). The golden vine was real. Josephus describes golden vines above the gate of the temple building itself, "from which clusters of grapes hung as tall as a man's height" (Jewish War 5.5.4), and says Herod's temple had "a golden vine, with its branches hanging down" over its doors (Antiquities 15.11.3). He also says that Aristobulus sent Pompey "a golden vine" worth five hundred talents (Antiquities 14.3.1). Music like Tacitus describes is not foreign to the Bible: David and Israel worshiped with "lyres, harps, hand drums, rattles and cymbals" (2 Samuel 6:5), Psalm 150:4 calls for "tambourine and dancing" and "reed pipe", and the Levite singers played lyres, harps and cymbals (1 Chronicles 15:16). The vine is also Israel's own picture (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1-7; John 15:1; see the topic on the vine). That is a link of imagery, not proof of what the temple's vine meant. A guess (Claude's, from no source): the booths feast, with its fruit and branches (Leviticus 23:40), could look like Dionysus's rites to Greek eyes. Differs. Tacitus himself rejects the Liber idea: Liber's rites are festive; "the Jewish way is absurd and sordid."
r: Leviticus 23:40-43; Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; John 15:1; 2 Samuel 6:5; Psalm 150:4; 1 Chronicles 15:16

a: Father Liber, the conqueror of the East
p: Liber is the Italian wine god, identified with the Greek Dionysus (Bacchus).
b: Roman writers matched Liber with Bacchus, who in Greek stories conquered the East. Tacitus gives the Liber idea only to reject it. The idea that the Jews worshiped Dionysus was a Greek and Roman guess; the Bible has no link. See the note on the golden vine.

a: the Jewish way is absurd and sordid
p: The Latin pair is harsh: absurd and filthy or mean.
b: Iudaeorum mos absurdus sordidusque. The Church and Brodribb English has "tasteless and mean." This site's translation keeps the insult, so the reader sees what a Roman historian wrote. A Christian reader may set it beside the Law as a contrast, not as an answer to the charge: "I show loyal love to thousands, for those who love me and keep my commands" (Exodus 20:6).

a: The country's eastern edge runs up against Arabia
p: Tacitus's map: Arabia east, Egypt south, Phoenicia and the sea west, Syria north.
b: The Bible's land is drawn with other markers, such as the boundaries in Numbers 34, but Tacitus gives a Roman's compass. Josephus, in the same war book, describes the Jericho plain and Dead Sea in the same way (Jewish War 4.8.3-4). The map explains why the Romans needed Syria's legions to deal with Judea.

a: there's balsam and palms
t: Balsam, palms and the City of Palms
p: Compared with the Bible: the Bible knows both the balm of Gilead and the City of Palms.
b: Josephus describes the plain of Jericho: palm trees "besides the balsam tree, whose ... fruits" are the most precious (Jewish War 4.8.3). The Bible has the "balm" Ishmaelite traders carried to Egypt (Genesis 37:25) and Jeremiah's cry, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22). Jericho is the "City of Palms" (Judges 1:16). Agrees with Tacitus on what the land produced. Tacitus's detail that the balsam tree's veins shrink back from iron and are opened with stone or pottery is his own and not found in Josephus's description read for this part.

a: The chief mountain is Libanus
p: Compared with the Bible: Moses asked to see "Lebanon" from across the Jordan.
b: Libanus is Lebanon. Tacitus notes the shade and snow in the heat, and that it feeds the Jordan. Moses prayed: "Please let me cross over and see the good land on the other side of the Jordan, that good hill country, and Lebanon" (Deuteronomy 3:25). The Jordan flows from the mountains of the far north (see the topic on the Jordan). Agrees in the geography. Tacitus's claim that Lebanon "feeds" the Jordan is the simplest reading; the river rises on Hermon, as the topic on the Jordan says.

a: it flows whole through one lake and another and is held in the third
t: The Jordan and its three lakes
p: Compared with the Bible: the Jordan ends in the Salt Sea, as Joshua says.
b: Tacitus counts three lakes. The Bible names the end: "The water flowing down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, was cut off completely" (Joshua 3:16), the same sea as the Valley of Siddim, "which is the Salt Sea" (Genesis 14:3). Agrees: the Jordan ends in a salt lake and does not reach the sea. The river was also the Israelites' crossing place in Joshua 3, which Tacitus never mentions in his Exodus story (5:3).

a: That lake is huge, looks like a sea, and tastes fouler
p: Compared with the Bible: the Salt Sea of Genesis 14 and Joshua 3; Ezekiel sees it healed.
b: Tacitus describes what the Bible calls the Salt Sea. Its water holds up what is thrown in, as Tacitus says; Josephus tells how Vespasian had non-swimmers thrown in with hands tied, and they floated (Jewish War 4.8.4). Ezekiel sees the opposite in a vision: a river from the temple flowing to the sea, where "the waters of the sea will be healed" and "There will be a huge number of fish" (Ezekiel 47:8-9). Agrees that no fish lived in it. See the topic on the Dead Sea.

a: At one season of the year it throws up bitumen
p: Compared with the Bible: Genesis 14 has "tar pits" in the Valley of Siddim; Josephus describes the lake's bitumen the same way.
b: "The Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits, pit after pit" (Genesis 14:10). Josephus: the lake "casts up black clods of bitumen" that float and are hauled into ships, and the bitumen is useful for caulking ships and in medicines (Jewish War 4.8.4). Agrees with Tacitus, who says that it shrinks from blood and that people who know the region say the floating masses are hauled ashore by hand and split with axes and wedges. Tacitus separates what "the old authors" say from what "people who know the region" report, a good habit of a historian.

a: plains that they say were once rich and home to great cities, until lightning struck and burned them
p: Compared with the Bible: this is the Genesis story of Sodom and Gomorrah told from outside, almost without names.
b: Genesis: "Lot raised his eyes and saw that the whole Plain of the Jordan was well watered all the way to Zoar, like the garden of the LORD" (Genesis 13:10), and then "the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, from the LORD, out of the sky" (Genesis 19:24). Tacitus has the rich plain, the many cities, fire from the sky. Josephus says nearly the same: the country of Sodom "was of old a most happy land" and "it was burnt by lightning" for the impiety of its people, with traces of the five cities still seen (Jewish War 4.8.4). Tacitus also says the land stays barren and its crops fail. Deuteronomy 29:23 describes such a land, "burned out with sulfur and salt, unsown, growing nothing", like Sodom and Gomorrah; the Wisdom of Solomon (a book some churches hold as Scripture) points to "a barren land that sends up smoke" and "plants whose fruit never fully ripens" (Wisdom of Solomon 10:7). Agrees on the event; differs in the cause: Genesis gives God's judgment and Tacitus gives the place's fumes. Strabo also reports local belief in thirteen cities, with Sodom as the chief one (Geography 16.2.44). This is the clearest case where a Roman writer preserves the Bible's account. See the topic on Sodom.
r: Genesis 13:10; Genesis 19:24-28; Deuteronomy 29:23; Wisdom of Solomon 10:6-7

a: I think the ground is poisoned by the lake's fumes
p: Tacitus grants the fire but explains the barren soil by the lake's fumes.
b: The Latin has ego ... concesserim, "I would grant": Tacitus allows that famous cities burned by "heavenly fire" and gives his own reason the land stays barren. This is rare, a personal opinion in the middle of a description. He neither denies the story nor credits the Bible's cause (see Genesis 19:24, "from the LORD"). Claude's view: it fits his pattern in this book of reporting a sacred story and offering a natural cause beside it, as with the water in 5:3 and the omens in 5:13.

a: The river Belus also runs into the Jewish Sea
t: The Belus and the glass sand
p: Josephus describes the same little river and its glass sand near Ptolemais (Acco).
b: Josephus describes the Belus near Ptolemais: a round hollow "affords such sand as glass is made of", which the winds refill (Jewish War 2.10.2). Ptolemais is the Acco of Judges 1:31; Paul's voyage stopped there for a day (Acts 21:7). Tacitus's "Jewish Sea" means the coast of the Mediterranean off Judea. The word for the mix is nitrum. Link strength: geography only.

a: Jerusalem is the nation's capital
p: Compared with the Bible: Jerusalem is the capital since David, and the Gospels' center.
b: "Hierosolyma genti caput": Jerusalem is the head of the nation. The Bible has it from David (see the topic on Jerusalem), and the Gospels, John and Acts center on it. Jesus weeps over it (Luke 19:41) and says it kills the prophets (Matthew 23:37). Tacitus's count of villages and towns across Judea fits the Gospels' picture of Jesus going "around the villages nearby, teaching" (Mark 6:6).

a: There stood a temple of immense wealth
p: Compared with the Bible: this is the temple of the Gospels, the one Jesus said would fall.
b: It was Herod's rebuilding of the second temple. John has the Jews say, "Forty-six years this temple was under construction" (John 2:20). A disciple says, "Look! Such stones! Such buildings!" and Jesus answers, "Here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Mark 13:1-2). Tacitus lists "immense wealth" in the same place; its capture is where his lost pages would have ended. Josephus gives the burning of the temple in Jewish War 6. Tacitus's temple is the one of the Gospels and Acts (see the topics on the temple and the second temple).

a: Only a Jew could come up to its doors, and everyone except priests was kept back from the threshold
p: Compared with the Bible: Acts shows the outer barrier in action.
b: The temple had courts with limits. Josephus says a stone partition around the inner court carried pillars with the law of purity "in Greek, and some in Roman letters", that "no foreigner should go within that sanctuary" (Jewish War 5.5.2). He has Titus recall these warnings and say the Jews were allowed to kill anyone who crossed the wall, "though he were a Roman" (6.2.4). In Acts, a mob cries that Paul "has brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place common" (Acts 21:28), having seen Trophimus of Ephesus in the city. Paul writes that Christ "broke down the middle wall, the wall that fenced us apart" (Ephesians 2:14); many readers take that wall to be the temple barrier, but Paul does not say so, and that is a reading. Agrees with Tacitus's picture of a closed temple, and with the Law's rule that only priests enter the holy place. See the topic on the dividing wall.

a: While the East belonged to the Assyrians, the Medes and the Persians, the Jews were the most despised of the subject peoples
p: Compared with the Bible: Assyria, Babylon (omitted), Media and Persia are the Bible's empires. Tacitus leaves out Babylon.
b: Tacitus names Assyria, Media and Persia and skips Babylon, which destroyed Solomon's temple (2 Kings 25). In the Bible, Assyria takes the northern kingdom, Cyrus the Persian lets the exiles go home (Ezra 1), and Persian rule is the setting of Ezra, Nehemiah and Esther. The "despised" label is Tacitus's. Haman's words in Esther 3:8 show a Persian official thinking the same. See the topics on Assyria, Persia and the Medes.

a: King Antiochus tried to strip away their superstition and give them Greek ways
t: King Antiochus and the ban on the Law
p: Compared with the Bible: 1 Maccabees tells a Greek attempt of the same kind, as persecution.
b: Tacitus names only "king Antiochus", and the Parthian war he mentions does not appear in 1 Maccabees. The site takes him to be Antiochus Epiphanes, the king of 1 Maccabees 1:10, because the attempt Tacitus describes, to change the Jews' customs, is the one that book tells; Josephus also names Antiochus Epiphanes as the king who spoiled the temple (Against Apion 2.7). 1 Maccabees: the king wrote that "each was to give up his own customs" (1 Maccabees 1:42), and "they built an abomination of desolation on the altar" (1 Maccabees 1:54). Daniel foretold the same: "set up the abomination that desolates" (Daniel 11:31). Tacitus calls the Jewish faith "superstition" (Latin superstitio, a Roman word for excessive, foreign religion) and thinks Antiochus would have improved "the vilest of nations". Same event, opposite verdict. 1 Maccabees is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches and is not accepted by Jews or most Protestants. See the topics on the Maccabean revolt and the Seleucids.

a: the war with the Parthians kept him from changing this vilest of nations
p: The Latin taeterrimam gentem is strong. The translation keeps it.
b: Taeterrimam gentem: the foulest or most hideous people. The translation keeps the strong word. Tacitus's claim that a Parthian war stopped Antiochus differs from 1 Maccabees. There the king goes east for money, fails to take a rich temple, and dies in grief (1 Maccabees 3:31; 1 Maccabees 6:1-4). Josephus says Antiochus took the temple's gold because he needed money (Against Apion 2.7). The sources agree he went east; they differ on why.

a: the Jews set up kings for themselves
p: Compared with the Bible: the Hasmonean kings were priests, but the Bible promises kingship to Judah.
b: After the Maccabean revolt the Hasmonean family, priests, took the royal title (see the topic on the Hasmoneans). Josephus says the first of them to wear a diadem, Aristobulus, was cruel to his mother and brothers (Antiquities 13.11). Alexander Jannaeus was pelted with citrons by the crowd at the festival of booths (Antiquities 13.13.5), which matches Tacitus's "driven out by the fickle crowd". Agrees with Tacitus on the cruelty and the crowd. Genesis 49:10 gives the scepter to Judah, not to a priestly family; this is one reason many Jews of the time looked for a Davidic king (see the topic on the Davidic covenant).

a: they took the honor of the priesthood as the foundation of their power
p: The Hasmoneans joined the high priesthood to the crown; Tacitus sees it as strategy.
b: Tacitus's reading is that the kings "fostered the superstition" because priestly honor was their basis. The Latin is quia honor sacerdotii firmamentum potentiae adsumebatur. The Bible keeps the roles apart: Levi's family for priesthood, David's for kingship (see the topics on priesthood and kingship). A Christian reader sees in this joining of offices a pattern Hebrews says Christ fulfills in a different way (Hebrews 7 is the passage; see the topic on Melchizedek).

a: Gnaeus Pompeius (Pompey) was the first Roman to conquer the Jews
p: Compared with the Bible: Pompey's conquest began the Roman rule of the Gospels' world.
b: Josephus tells how Pompey took the temple area and went into the sanctuary (Jewish War 1.7.6). The Jews of Jesus' day lived under the result: Rome's rule through Herod and then governors (see the topics on Rome and the Herod family). Before that, the Jews had a treaty with Rome (1 Maccabees 8). The site's topic on Rome notes this arc. Agrees with Tacitus: Pompey was the first.

a: an empty seat with no image of any god inside
p: Compared with the Bible: the holy of holies held no idol, but Josephus says it was not empty.
b: Tacitus says what Pompey found was an empty seat, no image of any god, secret rooms with nothing in them. Josephus and Tacitus can both be right. Josephus says Pompey and his men saw "the candlestick with its lamps, and the table, and the pouring vessels, and the censers, all made entirely of gold" and two thousand talents of sacred money, which he did not touch (Jewish War 1.7.6). Those stood in the outer part of the sanctuary; of the inmost room, the Holy of Holies, he says "In this there was nothing at all" (5.5.5). Cassius Dio says the Jews "never had any statue of him even in Jerusalem itself" (Roman History 37.17). In Against Apion Josephus answers the ass-head slander: Pompey, Crassus and Titus found nothing ridiculous (2.7). Agrees: no image, as the Law commands (Exodus 20:4). Differs only in the word "nothing": the furniture was there, and Solomon's inner room held two carved cherubim (1 Kings 6:23) over the ark's lid (Exodus 25:18-20). Solomon spoke of God as dwelling "in the thick dark cloud" (1 Kings 8:12). A Christian may also read the empty seat as a picture of a God who is not carved. The Gospels say the curtain was split when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51).

a: Pacorus, king of the Parthians, took Judea
p: Parthians held Judea briefly before Herod won it with Roman help.
b: Josephus tells of Pacorus, the Parthian king's son, sent into Judea (Jewish War 1.13; see also the Antiquities parallel). His Roman opponents were Publius Ventidius and Gaius Sosius. Tacitus gives the order right in outline: Parthians in, Parthians out, Sosius takes Jerusalem for Rome and Herod. Matthew's Herod is the man who came out of this: "Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea while Herod was king" (Matthew 2:1).

a: The kingdom Antony had given Herod, Augustus enlarged after his victory
p: Compared with the Bible: this is the Herod of Matthew 2 and Luke 1:5.
b: Same person? Very likely: Tacitus's Herod, king by Antony's gift and enlarged by Augustus, is Herod the Great, the king of Judea in Matthew 2:1 and Luke 1:5. The Gospels' Herod is "alarmed" at the news of a newborn king (Matthew 2:3). Tacitus's Antony and Augustus also form the background of Luke's "an order came out from Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1). See the topic on the Herod family.

a: a man named Simon, without waiting for the emperor, seized the royal title
p: Josephus tells of a rebel Simon who took the crown after Herod's death, but he says Gratus killed him.
b: Josephus: "Simon, one of the servants to the king ... put a diadem upon his own head," burned the royal palace at Jericho, and was cut down by Gratus, captain of the king's foot (Jewish War 2.4.2). Tacitus says Quintilius Varus punished him. Differs: Josephus names Gratus. Josephus also tells how Varus put down the larger revolt in Judea after Herod's death. The uprisings after Herod's death are the background of Archelaus's rule: "Archelaus now ruled Judea in place of his father Herod" (Matthew 2:22). Link: not the Simon of any Bible book.

a: the nation, held in check, was ruled in three parts by Herod's children
p: Compared with the Bible: Archelaus, Antipas and Philip, as in Matthew 2 and Luke 3:1.
b: After Herod the realm went to his sons. Matthew names Archelaus ruling Judea (Matthew 2:22), and Luke 3:1 names "Herod ruled Galilee as tetrarch, his brother Philip ruled the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis." Agrees exactly. Tacitus does not name them. See the topic on the Herod family.

a: Under Tiberius it was quiet
p: Compared with the Bible: the quiet is the years of Jesus' ministry and death, which Tacitus passes over in three words.
b: Tacitus's Latin is sub Tiberio quies. Those years are the ministry of John, Jesus and the early church: "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule. Pontius Pilate was governing Judea" (Luke 3:1). Jesus died under Pilate. Tacitus knows this: in the Annals he writes that Christus "suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus" (Annals 15.44, in Church and Brodribb's wording). So in the Histories he does not mention it, because his Jewish excursus is about the nation, not the movement. Strengths and limits: Tacitus was not a Christian writer, which is why his line is used as an outside witness; but he wrote decades after the event, and the Annals passage does not say where he got it. See the topic on Pontius Pilate.

a: Then, when they were ordered by Caligula to put his statue in the temple, they took up arms rather than do it
p: Josephus and Philo both tell of the order to put the emperor's statue in the temple.
b: Josephus's chapter on it (Jewish War 2.10) carries the heading, in Whiston's English, "Caius Commands That His Statue Should Be Set Up In The Temple Itself", and he tells how the governor Petronius met Jews at Ptolemais who pleaded "first for their laws, and in the next place, for themselves." Philo of Alexandria also tells it (On the Embassy to Gaius). Caligula's death ended it. The Bible does not tell this episode, but the Gospels' "abomination of desolation" language (Mark 13:14) was read by some as pointing to such a threat. See the topic on the abomination of desolation.

a: Claudius, with the kings dead or cut down to little, handed the province of Judea to Roman Knights or freedmen (former slaves)
t: Claudius and the end of Agrippa I
p: Compared with the Bible: Acts 12 records the death of the last real Jewish king; Claudius also appears at Acts 11:28 and Acts 18:2.
b: Tacitus says Claudius gave Judea to Roman Knights or freedmen. Acts has the death of King Herod Agrippa I at Caesarea: "an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give the glory to God" (Acts 12:23). After that Judea was under procurators again. Other Claudius events in Acts: the famine Agabus foretold, "in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28), and the order that "all the Jews must leave Rome" (Acts 18:2); Suetonius says Claudius banished the Jews from Rome for disturbances "at the instigation of one Chrestus" (Claudius 25). Agrees. See the topics on famine and Priscilla and Aquila.

a: Antonius Felix
p: Compared with the Bible: Tacitus's Antonius Felix is very likely the Felix before whom Paul was tried.
b: Same person? Very likely. For: same name, same office, same province, same period, and the Bible adds more. Josephus: "Claudius sent Felix, the brother of Pallas, to take care of the affairs of Judea" (Antiquities 20.7.1), and in Tacitus's Annals the Felix of Judea is the brother of Pallas (Annals 12.54). Suetonius: Claudius made Felix governor of Judea, and he became "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28). Acts: Lysias sends Paul "through safely to Felix, the governor" (Acts 23:24); Paul says to him, "you have sat as judge over this nation for many years" (Acts 24:10); and after "Two full years" Porcius Festus took over (Acts 24:27). Against: one difference of order. In the Annals, Felix already governs Samaria while Cumanus governs Galilee (Annals 12.54); in Josephus, Felix is sent after Claudius banishes Cumanus (Antiquities 20.6.3; 20.7.1). Tacitus's different Drusilla is the other difficulty (next note). Who argued it: William Whiston's footnote to Antiquities 20.7.2 treats Tacitus's Felix as the same man and only his wife as mixed up.

a: using every kind of cruelty and lust, exercised a king's power with a slave's mind
t: Felix's character in Acts and Josephus
p: Compared with the Bible: Acts shows a governor who is afraid, greedy and unjust. Josephus shows the cruelty.
b: Tacitus: per omnem saevitiam ac libidinem ius regium servili ingenio exercuit. The Latin servili ingenio, "with a slave's mind", is a figure of speech about Felix's character. As for his birth, Suetonius lists Felix among Claudius's freedmen (Claudius 28), and Tacitus's Annals call his brother Pallas a freedman (Annals 12.53, 12.54). In Acts: Tertullus flatters him ("Thanks to you, we live in great peace", Acts 24:2); Paul talks of "righteousness, ... self-control and ... the judgment that lies ahead, and Felix became afraid" (Acts 24:25); he "was also hoping, all the while, that Paul would hand him some money" (Acts 24:26); and he "left Paul behind in chains" to please the Jews (Acts 24:27). Josephus adds that Felix's troops destroyed a great number of followers of a false prophet and put down "the Egyptian" (Jewish War 2.13.5), whom the Roman commander in Jerusalem also mentions (Acts 21:38). Agrees that Felix was corrupt and easily afraid; the Bible gives less cruelty, but it records a man who left an innocent man in prison for money and favor. Tacitus's Annals also says Felix thought "he could do any evil act with impunity."

a: He had married Drusilla, granddaughter of Cleopatra and Antony
t: Which Drusilla? Tacitus and Acts differ
p: Compared with the Bible: Acts' Drusilla is Jewish; Tacitus's is Cleopatra's granddaughter. Probably two wives.
b: Acts: "Felix came with Drusilla, his own wife, a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24). Josephus: this Drusilla was a sister of Agrippa II. She had married Azizus, king of Emesa, who agreed to be circumcised; Felix fell in love with her and sent a Cypriot Jew named Simon to persuade her to leave her husband, and she married Felix and had a son, Agrippa (Antiquities 20.7.1-2). Tacitus: his Drusilla is a granddaughter of Cleopatra and Antony. Suetonius: Felix was "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28). Two views agree that Felix had more than one wife: the editor of the Thomson-Forester Suetonius (footnote 537) says two of Felix's wives were named Drusilla, the Jewish sister of Agrippa and a granddaughter of Cleopatra and Antony; Whiston, in his note on Antiquities 20.7.2, also accepts that Felix married such a granddaughter, and thinks Tacitus, finding the name Drusilla on one of them, "mistook her for that other wife, whose name he did not know." The difference is only whether Tacitus knew the two wives were different women. Verdict on the Bible: nothing in Tacitus contradicts Acts, because he never says who Felix's wife was in the 50s. The site's judgment is that two wives named Drusilla is the likelier reading.

a: so Felix was Antony's grandson-in-law, while Claudius was Antony's grandson
p: Tacitus makes Felix and Claudius family of Antony's line.
b: Tacitus says Claudius was Antony's grandson (the Latin is Claudius nepos esset). The joke of the sentence is that a freedman became the emperor's kinsman through marriage. Suetonius names such favorites among Claudius's freedmen: Posides, then Felix, Harpocras, Polybius, Narcissus and Pallas (Claudius 28). It shows why Tacitus calls Felix servile: he was a favorite of a court run by freedmen.

a: Roman Knights or freedmen
t: Roman Knights and freedmen as governors
p: Tacitus says Claudius gave Judea to Roman Knights or freedmen, and names Felix among them.
b: The "Roman Knights" were the class just below senators. Tacitus calls Pilate "one of our procurators" in the Annals (see the topic on Pontius Pilate). Felix was a freedman (a former slave) who became governor: Suetonius lists him among Claudius's freedmen (Claudius 28), an unusual step Tacitus mocks. The Bible's word for these governors is the Greek hegemon ("governor"): Pilate (Luke 3:1) and Felix (Acts 23:24).

a: the two kings
p: Compared with the Bible: Acts 25-26 names Bernice beside Agrippa; later writers link her with Titus.
b: Tacitus names Agrippa here but not his sister. Acts adds his sister: "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice" (Acts 25:13), and "Agrippa and Bernice arrived in grand display" (Acts 25:23). Josephus names her as the daughter of Agrippa I who was twice married and was rumored to be too close to her brother (Antiquities 20.7.3). Suetonius tells of Titus's "well-known attachment to queen Berenice, who received from him, as it is reported, a promise of marriage", and says that when Titus became emperor he "immediately sent away Berenice from the city, much against both their inclinations" (Titus 7, Thomson-Forester English). The editor's footnote there adds, from Xiphilinus, that she lived in Rome with Titus "to all appearance, as his wife." Same person as Berenice? Very likely: "Bernice" is the Greek form, "Berenice" the Latin one, and Josephus and Acts describe the same sister of Agrippa.

a: Gessius Florus was procurator
p: The procurator whose rule, in Josephus's telling, pushed the Jews into revolt.
b: A procurator was the emperor's agent in charge of a province. Josephus gives Florus a chapter of his own (Jewish War 2.14), headed in Whiston's English as the governor who "by the barbarity of his government forces the Jews into the war." Tacitus agrees that war began under him but says nothing of the cause. Felix, Festus and Albinus came before him (Acts 24:27 names Festus replacing Felix). Link: Florus is not in the Bible; the Bible's last governors are Felix and Festus (Acts 23-26).

a: Cestius Gallus, the legate of Syria
p: The governor of Syria whose army was beaten near Jerusalem; Suetonius says the Jews took a legion's eagle.
b: A legate was a Roman governor with an army. Josephus tells the retreat of Cestius at length (Jewish War 2.19); Whiston's chapter heading says Cestius retreated "without any just occasion in the world." Suetonius writes that the Jews "routed the lieutenant of Syria, a man of consular rank," and took an eagle (Vespasian 4). This defeat explains why the 12th legion had a score to settle (Jewish War 5.1.6; see 5:1). Cestius is not in the Bible.

a: Nero sent Vespasian
t: Vespasian and the end of Nero's reign
p: Compared with the Bible: Nero is the emperor of Paul's final years; Vespasian's war is the war Jesus foretold.
b: Suetonius says Vespasian was chosen for the Judean war for his proven skill and because his low birth made him no danger (Vespasian 4). Nero is the emperor to whom Paul appealed (Acts 25:11, "I appeal to Caesar!"), whose Rome saw Paul in custody (Acts 28:16). Josephus and Suetonius name the same stages, and Suetonius adds a Nero story: astrologers told him that after losing power he would get "the rule of the East" and some said "the kingdom of Jerusalem" (Nero 40). See the topic on Nero.

a: It made us angrier that the Jews alone hadn't given in
t: Why Rome wanted this war finished
p: Tacitus: Rome's anger grew because the Jews alone had not given in.
b: The Latin is augebat iras quod soli Iudaei non cessissent. Tacitus speaks as a Roman ("us"). Josephus's version is that Jewish rebels refused to quit. Jesus' own words look at the same nation: "If only you too had recognized on this day what leads to peace!" (Luke 19:42). The Sanhedrin's fear in John is the Roman mind in a Jewish mouth: "Then the Romans will come and take from us our place and our nation alike" (John 11:48). Link: background.

a: in case anything happened under the new regime
p: Titus stayed with the armies because the Flavians' power was new.
b: Vespasian had just won the empire (the civil war is Books 1-4). Keeping his son in command of a big army was a safety measure, and gave the new dynasty its first great victory. The Latin says a new rule (novi principatus) might bring chance events, so the prince's son stayed with the main army.

a: Two hills of enormous height
p: Compared with the Bible: Jerusalem stands on hills the Bible calls Zion; Josephus counts two main hills.
b: Josephus: "The city was built upon two hills ... that which contains the upper city is much higher", called the "Citadel" by king David (Jewish War 5.4.1). Psalm 76:2 puts God's "den in Zion." Tacitus's "two hills of enormous height" is the same pair. See the topic on Mount Zion. Tacitus and Josephus give the picture of a naturally strong site, which makes the Romans' choice of a siege understandable.

a: the towers rose to sixty feet where the hill helped, and to 120 feet where the ground dropped away
p: Tacitus gives feet; Josephus gives cubits for the three great towers.
b: Josephus measures Herod's towers: Hippicus 80 cubits and Phasael about 90 (Jewish War 5.4.3). A Roman writer using feet and a Jewish one using cubits do not compare easily, and Tacitus's numbers describe the walls, not the three named towers. The figures in the Latin are sexagenos pedes (sixty feet each) and centenos vicenosque (120 each). No Bible passage gives these heights.

a: the tower Antonia, named by Herod in honor of Marcus Antonius
t: The Antonia tower and Paul's arrest
p: Compared with the Bible: this fortress is the "barracks" where the Romans took Paul in Acts 21.
b: Josephus: Herod rebuilt a fortress at the temple and "gratified Antonius, who was his friend, and the Roman ruler, and then gave it the name of the Tower of Antonia" (Antiquities 15.11.4), and it stood at a corner of the temple courts with a Roman guard (Jewish War 5.5.8). In Acts, when a mob tried to kill Paul, "a report went up to the commander of the cohort" and Paul was taken "into the barracks" (Acts 21:31, 34); "By the time he got to the stairs," the soldiers were carrying him (Acts 21:35). Josephus says the Antonia had passages down into the temple cloisters, through which the Roman guard went among the people on festivals (Jewish War 5.5.8). That fits the stairs and the garrison of Acts, so the site takes the barracks to be the Antonia (an inference from these two texts). Agrees. This is the building from which the Roman commander watched the temple crowds. Josephus later says the Jews tore it down (Jewish War 6.5.4), the step he links with an "oracle" that the temple would be taken when it became square.

a: It didn't seem worthy of them to wait for the enemy to starve.
p: Tacitus says the Romans meant to storm the city; Jesus describes a siege.
b: Tacitus presents a Roman wish to attack at once because starving a city seemed unworthy. Luke 19:43 describes the opposite plan: "your enemies will put up a palisade of stakes against you. They will ring you round and press in on you from every side." At 5:13 Tacitus himself says Titus chose "earthworks and covered shelters" because the ground ruled out a rush. My reading (spec): the two Roman descriptions agree with Luke's wording once Titus changes plan; Josephus has a chapter on how Titus "thought fit to encompass the city round with a wall" (Jewish War 5.12), which fits "ring you round".

a: The very colonnades around the temple
p: Compared with the Bible: Jesus and the apostles taught in the temple colonnades.
b: Jesus "was walking around in the temple, in Solomon's Porch" (John 10:23), and the apostles "all used to gather in Solomon's Porch" (Acts 5:12). Tacitus sees these long porticoes as military walls; the Gospels see them as meeting places. Josephus describes the temple's cloisters as supported by large pillars (Jewish War 5.5.2). Agrees on the structure.

a: a spring that never ran dry, hills hollowed out underground, and pools and cisterns for saving rain
p: Tacitus lists the city's water supply. Josephus names the spring of Siloam.
b: Josephus says of the valley between the two hills that it "extended as far as Siloam; for that is the name of a fountain which hath sweet water in it, and this in great plenty" (Jewish War 5.4.1). Tacitus's "spring that never ran dry" is likely this water. Second Kings tells how Hezekiah "made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city" (2 Kings 20:20).

a: they bought the right to fortify
p: Josephus says Agrippa I began the Bezetha wall and stopped for fear of Claudius.
b: Tacitus blames "the greed of the Claudian years" for the Jews' being able to buy permission. Josephus tells a different story: the father of the present Agrippa "began that wall we spoke of; but he left off building it when he had only laid the foundations, out of the fear he was in of Claudius Caesar" (Jewish War 5.4.2). Differs. Both agree the wall was begun under Claudius. The Agrippa of Josephus is Agrippa I, who died in Acts 12.

a: Simon held the outermost and widest walls
p: Josephus names Simon son of Gioras and says he held the upper city and much of the lower.
b: Josephus: "the tyrant Simon, the son of Gioras, whom the people had invited in ... having in his power the upper city, and a great part of the lower" (Jewish War 5.1.3). Tacitus puts him on the outer walls. Neither man is in the Bible. The name "Bargioras" is Simon's name (bar Gioras, "son of Gioras"); Tacitus gives it to John (next note).

a: Bargioras
p: Tacitus gives John of Gischala the name Josephus gives to Simon.
b: Josephus calls John's rival "Simon, the son of Gioras" (Jewish War 5.1.3) and John another man, who "never left off murdering" (5.1.2). Tacitus's "John, whom they also called Bargioras" mixes the two names. This is a fair example of how a Roman historian working from reports, not from the Jewish side, could get a Jewish name wrong. It is no Bible passage; bar is Aramaic for "son of" and appears in the Bible in names such as Bar-Jesus (Acts 13:6).

a: Eleazar had fortified the temple
p: Josephus: Eleazar son of Simon held the inner court of the temple.
b: Josephus: Eleazar, son of Simon, "made the first separation of the zealots from the people", withdrew into the temple, and with others seized "the inner court of the temple" (Jewish War 5.1.2). The Bible names rebels of earlier years too: Simon "called the Zealot" (Luke 6:15), Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), Barabbas, held "with the rebels who had killed people during the uprising" (Mark 15:7), and the "Sicarii" led out by "that Egyptian" (Acts 21:38).
