a: a great store of grain was burned
p: Josephus says the factions burned the stores that could have fed a siege for years.
b: Josephus: "almost all that corn was burnt, which would have been sufficient for a siege of many years. So they were taken by the means of the famine" (Jewish War 5.1.4). Agrees with Tacitus. Luke 21:11 lists famines among the signs. See the topic on famine.

a: John sent men under cover of offering a sacrifice, to cut down Eleazar and his band, and took the temple
t: John's seizure of the temple at Passover
p: Compared with the Bible: Josephus dates it to the feast of unleavened bread, the Exodus festival.
b: Josephus: on "the feast of unleavened bread ... when it is believed the Jews were first freed from the Egyptians," Eleazar opened the gates to worshipers, and John "made use of this festival as a cloak for his treacherous designs" and armed men with weapons hidden under their garments (Jewish War 5.3.1). Tacitus says "under cover of offering a sacrifice" and does not name the feast. Agrees in the trick; Josephus adds the feast and the deaths among worshipers. The festival is Passover (see the note on 5:4 and the topic on Passover): the day Israel remembers its rescue from Egypt is the day the temple is turned into a battlefield.

a: the city split into two factions, until the Romans' approach brought harmony out of a foreign war
p: Compared with the Bible: Jesus' warning about a divided house, and the prophets' view of Jerusalem's judgment.
b: Tacitus: donec propinquantibus Romanis bellum externum concordiam pareret, "until a foreign war brought harmony." Josephus, reflecting on the same facts, writes that the three-way split was "a good thing, and the effect of Divine justice" (Jewish War 5.1.1). Jesus said, "Look, your house is abandoned to you, deserted" (Matthew 23:38). A Christian reader may see all three accounts describing one judgment. Tacitus does not say so; he just calls the unity forced.

a: Armies were seen clashing across the sky, weapons glowing red
t: Omens before the war: Tacitus, Josephus and Jesus
p: Compared with the Bible: Josephus lists the same signs; Jesus spoke of great signs from the sky.
b: Josephus tells of a star like a sword over the city, a great light at the altar, a heifer giving birth to a lamb in the temple, and "chariots and troops of soldiers in their armor ... running about among the clouds, and surrounding of cities" (Jewish War 6.5.3). He places these before the war, not during the siege, and says the learned read them as a warning. Tacitus puts them just before the siege and gives the Jews' response as stubbornness. Jesus said: "There will be terrors, and great signs from the sky" (Luke 21:11), and "there will be signs in the sun, the moon and the stars" (Luke 21:25). Link strength: thematic. Josephus does not mention Jesus' prophecy. See the topic on cosmic signs and the Olivet discourse.

a: the temple suddenly lit by fire from the clouds
p: Josephus tells of a light on the altar at the Passover feast.
b: Josephus: "so great a light shone round the altar and the holy house, that it appeared to be bright day time; which lasted for half an hour" at the feast of unleavened bread (Jewish War 6.5.3). Tacitus's "fire from the clouds" is a different picture of a similar night sign.

a: The doors of the shrine swung open all at once
p: Josephus names the eastern gate of the inner temple.
b: Josephus: the brass eastern gate of the inner court, which twenty men could hardly close, "was seen to be opened of its own accord about the sixth hour of the night" (Jewish War 6.5.3). He adds that the common people took it as lucky, but the learned understood that the temple's security "was dissolved of its own accord." Tacitus says the shrine doors opened and links it with a departing voice. Same event, two reports.

a: a voice louder than any human voice was heard saying the gods were leaving
t: "The gods are leaving" and "Let us remove hence"
p: Compared with the Bible: Josephus gives the voice; Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the first temple.
b: Tacitus: excedere deos, "the gods are going out." Josephus says that at Pentecost the priests felt a quaking and heard "a sound as of a great multitude, saying, 'Let us remove hence'" (Jewish War 6.5.3). The older Bible picture is Ezekiel's vision: "The glory of the LORD went up from the middle of the city and stood on the mountain east of the city" (Ezekiel 11:23; Ezekiel 10:18-19), before the first temple fell. Agrees that the sign was a departure. Tacitus has "the gods" plural, as a Roman would, where a Jewish source would have one God. A Christian reader may also hear Jesus' words, "your house is abandoned to you" (Matthew 23:38). Neither Tacitus nor Josephus makes the link.

a: prone to superstition but hostile to religious rites, didn't think it right to make up for with sacrifices or vows
p: Latin: gens superstitioni obnoxia, religionibus adversa. Tacitus calls Jews superstitious and also against religion.
b: Superstitio was the Roman word for religion of the wrong kind, too anxious or too foreign. Religiones were the proper rites of the state, with sacrifices (hostiae) and vows (vota) that the Romans used to turn away bad omens. Tacitus means that Jews would not use Roman methods. The complaint is the same as in 5:5: the Jews do not honor the gods of the state. A Christian reader sees the opposite: a people who will not make atonement to other gods.

a: the ancient writings of their priests said that at this very time the East would grow strong and men setting out from Judea would rule the world
p: Compared with the Bible: Josephus and Suetonius report it too. Christians read the ruler as Jesus.
b: The same oracle is in three Roman-era writers. Josephus: "an ambiguous oracle ... found in their sacred writings, how, 'about that time, one from their country should become governor of the habitable earth'" and he says it "certainly denoted the government of Vespasian" (Jewish War 6.5.4). Suetonius: "A firm persuasion had long prevailed through all the East, that it was fated for the empire of the world, at that time, to devolve on some who should go forth from Judaea" (Vespasian 4). Neither names a verse. Candidates in the Bible: "A star will march out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel" (Numbers 24:17); "The scepter will not leave Judah ... until Shiloh comes, and to him the peoples will give obedience" (Genesis 49:10); "one like a son of man" given rule over all peoples (Daniel 7:13-14). Christian reading: the promised ruler is Jesus, whom the magi called "the newborn king of the Jews" (Matthew 2:2); his rule is "a rule that lasts forever" (Daniel 7:14). Josephus's reading gives the oracle to Vespasian; Tacitus agrees (next note). Which verse lay behind the report is my guess, not a stated fact.
r: Numbers 24:17; Genesis 49:10; Daniel 7:13-14; Daniel 9:26; Matthew 2:1-2; Isaiah 9:6-7

a: Those riddles had really predicted Vespasian and Titus
p: Claude's theory: three writers hand the oracle to the Flavians, so an ambiguous promise is claimed by the winner.
b: Tacitus says the oracle pointed to Vespasian and Titus. Josephus says the same of Vespasian. Suetonius notes that the report "referred to a Roman emperor, as the event shewed; but the Jews, applying it to themselves, broke out into rebellion." For Josephus, a Jew who joined the Romans, it served as proof that God had sided with Rome. Spec (Claude's theory): the three Roman-era reports show that the promise of a ruler from Judea was widely known, and the Flavians used it. A Christian reader holds the Bible's promise was fulfilled in Jesus ("His kingdom will have no end", Luke 1:33), not in Vespasian; the Gospels also warn against rebel messiahs who "give great signs and wonders" (Matthew 24:24). This is my reading.

a: six hundred thousand
p: Compared with the Bible: Exodus 12:37 uses the same number for the men who left Egypt. Josephus uses it for something else.
b: Tacitus: sexcenta milia in the besieged, "we have been told." Josephus says that many eminent citizens who ran away to Titus told him "no fewer than six hundred thousand" of the poor had been thrown dead out of the gates (Jewish War 5.13.7). He totals those who perished "during the whole siege" at 1,100,000, and those carried captive "during this whole war" at 97,000; many of the dead had come "up from all the country to the feast of unleavened bread" (6.9.3). Exodus: "about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting the little ones" (Exodus 12:37). Spec: the match may be chance, or a round number used for "a great host." It may also have reached Tacitus from a report like Josephus's with the meaning changed. Nothing says Tacitus had Exodus in mind. Josephus's figure for the dead shows Tacitus's number is far lower than Josephus's total.

a: he decided to fight with earthworks and covered shelters for his men
t: Earthworks, shelters and the "palisade of stakes"
p: Compared with the Bible: Luke 19:43 describes the siege works.
b: The Latin is aggeribus vineisque: siege mounds and the light roofed shelters (vineae) that protected men working near a wall. Josephus has banks raised at several places by different legions (Jewish War 5.11.4). Luke 19:43: "your enemies will put up a palisade of stakes against you. They will ring you round and press in on you from every side." Agrees in kind. Josephus says Titus had a wall built around the whole city (Jewish War 5.12); Luke's "ring you round" fits that. See the topic on the siege of Jerusalem.

a: the Old Camp
p: A Roman legion base on the Rhine, in what is now Germany.
b: Vetera castra, "the Old Camp," was a legion fortress on the lower Rhine. In 5:25 the Batavian nobles recall the time "when the legions were besieged and the legates killed." It has no Bible link; it goes on the list of places for the atlas.

a: Meanwhile Civilis
p: Batavian noble who led the Rhine revolt; Tacitus tells his story across Books 4 and 5.
b: Tacitus tells the earlier part of Civilis's story in the other parts of the Histories. In Book 5 he rebuilds his army after a defeat among the Treveri (5:14), fights Cerialis, loses his ground, and at 5:26 asks for a talk. His own speech at 5:26 claims he took up arms for Vespasian. The Rhine war and the siege of Jerusalem happen in the same year (5:1, 5:23), and Tacitus switches between them. There is no Bible link; the story belongs to the Roman world of the Gospels' age, a generation after the cross.

a: his forces doubled
p: Church and Brodribb's English says the 6th; the Latin says the 13th.
b: The Latin reads secundae et tertiae decimae et quartae decimae, "the 2nd, the 13th and the 14th." The variant records the difference. The 6th legion appears at 5:16 in Cerialis's speech, as the one that made Galba emperor.

a: the Batavians
p: A Germanic people on an island between the Rhine and Waal who supplied Rome's soldiers.
b: Tacitus has Civilis's Batavians say in 5:25 that they are asked "only to supply courage and men" (Latin virtutem et viros), not tribute: they served in Rome's armies as allies, which is why this revolt hurt Rome.

a: more like a naval battle
p: The fight in the marsh is compared to a sea fight.
b: The Latin is tamquam navali pugna, "as if in a naval battle." The Latin has no "dry ground". Roman heavy infantry were at a disadvantage in water, Tacitus says at 5:14.

a: Gugerni
p: The Latin spells the Rhine tribe Cugerni; Church and Brodribb print Gugerni.
b: At 5:16 the Latin has Cugerni and at 5:18 Cugernos; the English edition has "Gugerni." The site keeps Church and Brodribb's spelling. This is a spelling difference only, so it has no variant entry.

a: Cerialis spoke of the old glory of the Roman name
p: A general's short talk, given unit by unit.
b: Tacitus says the talks were not one big speech but short words to each unit as the general rode up. Cerialis names the 14th ("the Conquerors of Britain"), says the 6th had made Galba emperor and says the 2nd would be first to dedicate a new eagle in this battle. The eagle was a legion's standard; Suetonius says the Jews took one from Cestius's army (Vespasian 4).

a: The Rhine and the gods of Germany are in sight
p: Compared with the Bible: other nations' gods in a pagan general's speech.
b: Civilis calls on the Rhine and the gods of Germany. The Bible treats such gods as "gods they had not known" and says what is sacrificed to them goes "to demons and not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20). Christian readers differ on whether those gods are empty or real powers (see the card in this site's other chapters and the topic on idolatry). Civilis here uses the gods to stir his men, as Roman generals used theirs. Link: background.

a: Drusus Germanicus
p: A dam on the Rhine built by Drusus, whom Tacitus names Drusus Germanicus.
b: Civilis tears down the dam, and the Rhine rushes toward Gaul. The site adds no Bible link. Suetonius says that Drusus, the father of the emperor Claudius, fought the German wars and "made likewise some prodigious trenches beyond the Rhine, which to this day are called by his name" (Claudius 1). Tacitus's dam is very likely a work of this Drusus, which would make the builder the father of the Claudius of Acts 11:28 and Acts 18:2. This verse does not say so.

a: Arenacum
p: Places on the lower Rhine and Waal where Civilis attacked in one day.
b: The places named are Arenacum, Batavodurum, Grinnes and Vada. None is in the Bible, and the atlas harvest has no data for books outside the 66. They are named here for any later map work.

a: Briganticus
p: Briganticus, Civilis's nephew, is among those killed.
b: The Latin says Civili avunculo infensum, "hostile to his uncle Civilis." There is no Bible link.

a: They had kept silent at first to avoid being noticed
p: The Perseus Latin has a stray space and comma in this sentence.
b: The printed Latin reads utque ad fallendum silentio , ita coepta caede, with a space before the comma, which looks like a dropped word. Church and Brodribb translate through it: "They sought at first to elude notice by silence, but when the slaughter was begun ... a deafening shout." The site's translation follows that sense.

a: an affair, most people believed, with an Ubian woman, Claudia Sacrata
t: Claudia Sacrata and Claudia in 2 Timothy
p: Compared with the Bible: 2 Timothy 4:21 greets Timothy from a woman named Claudia. A weak match.
b: Claudia Sacrata is an Ubian woman, Cerialis's alleged companion. 2 Timothy 4:21 sends greetings "from Eubulus, from Pudens, Linus and Claudia." Same person? Unlikely. Claudia was a very common Roman woman's name, the women live on different edges of the empire, and nothing but the name links them. Tacitus says only what "most people believed" and blames the sentries.

a: a gift for Veleda
p: The Germans tow the captured flagship up the Lupia as an offering.
b: The captured flagship is towed up the river Lupia as a gift for Veleda, a seer of the German tribes. At 5:24 Cerialis writes to "Veleda and her relatives," and at 5:25 the Batavian nobles prefer Rome's emperors to "the women of the Germans." The Bible knows women prophets: Deborah, who was judging Israel (Judges 4:4), and Huldah, whom the king's officers consulted (2 Kings 22:14). Contrast: they speak for the LORD; Veleda speaks for the gods of her people. A captured sacred prize also appears in the Bible: "The Philistines took up God's ark, brought it into the house of Dagon" (1 Samuel 5:2). The likeness is only that captured sacred objects become trophies.

a: a huge number of small boats
p: Church and Brodribb print three or four hundred; the Latin says thirty or forty.
b: The Latin is tricenos quadragenosque. A Liburnian was a light, fast galley. Thirty or forty men fits a small boat; a figure of hundreds does not. The variant on this verse records the difference.

a: as autumn turned and the rains around the equinox came heavy
p: A date marker: the Rhine campaign ends in the autumn of the year Titus besieged Jerusalem.
b: Tacitus dates the end of Cerialis's campaign to the autumn rains. The same year had the siege of Jerusalem (5:1 says it began in the same year). Josephus tells the siege in his Books 5 and 6.

a: Cerialis, through secret messengers, held out peace to the Batavians and pardon to Civilis
p: Peace for the Batavians, pardon for Civilis, a push on Veleda.
b: Cerialis's message works by splitting the rebels: it offers the Batavians peace, tells Veleda her family should do Rome a service, and warns Civilis that exile means being a burden. The next verse shows the effect: the Batavians turn on Civilis. A Christian reader may compare Titus's offers to Jerusalem's defenders, which Josephus records (Jewish War 5.9, where he is sent to urge peace), without the same result.

a: One nation can't push back the slavery of the whole world
t: Why one nation can't fight Rome
p: Compared with the Bible: the Sanhedrin in John 11:48 reasons the same way about Rome.
b: The Batavian commoners argue that a single nation cannot beat the world's rulers, and that, unlike the Raetians, the Noricans and the other allies who carry heavy burdens, the Batavians pay no tribute but supply courage and men. This is the fear that moved Jerusalem's leaders before the cross: "If we leave him alone like this, everyone will believe in him. Then the Romans will come and take from us our place and our nation alike" (John 11:48). In the Gospels the tax itself is the issue: "Is it permitted to pay the head tax to Caesar, or not?" (Mark 12:14). Link: thematic.

a: more honorable to put up with the emperors of the Romans than with the women of the Germans
p: An insult aimed at Veleda and her circle.
b: The Latin is honestius principes Romanorum quam Germanorum feminas tolerari. It is a Roman-side point that being ruled by a seer's women is worse than being ruled by emperors. The Bible's account of women who judged and prophesied (Judges 4:4) shows a different view of such leaders.

a: Aponius in Moesia and Flavianus in Pannonia
p: The surviving text stops in the middle of a sentence.
b: The sentence ends "...Aponius in Moesia and Flavianus in Pannonia" and the manuscript stops there. Wikipedia's summary of the Histories says only the first four books and the first 26 chapters of the fifth survive. So Tacitus's account of the end of the Batavian revolt, and of the fall of Jerusalem, is lost. The site's text follows the Perseus edition, which ends here.

a: Primus Antonius knew this, and his letters pushed me into the war
p: Civilis says the letters of Primus Antonius, and Hordeonius Flaccus in person, urged him to take arms.
b: Civilis presents his revolt as part of the Flavian rising, with Mucianus in Syria, Aponius in Moesia and Flavianus in Pannonia. Tacitus lets him argue it, but the Batavian nobles had said at 5:25 that the war was his own rage. Compare 5:24: "Civilis claimed that the legions could have been crushed." The reader must weigh a man defending himself.
